review.title: HIDA after equivocal gallbladder ultrasound

cues.phrase: The common duct is not dilated; bilirubin is within the laboratory reference range.
cues.why: This paired negative lowers the appeal of the duct-imaging distractor. It is medically meaningful localization, not a sufficient nonmedical route to distinguish the two scintigraphy protocols; retain it rather than manufacture duct uncertainty.

fairness: Review scope for this entire report: 73 current after versions, including 30 contextRevisions. Only Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task and Options inform item judgments; basic metadata informs only basicVerdict. Previous verdicts, rationales and future results confer no credit. Difficulty is an uncalibrated PGY-2/3 prediction; this offline review is not clinical approval or current-source verification.

The key is defensible among the offered protocols: interpret persistent inflammatory features despite incomplete sonographic support, then distinguish gallbladder filling from stimulated function testing. A stone alone does not supply that distinction.
No conspicuous option-length, grammar or unique stem-to-key wording shortcut. The preserved ultrasound components are better than an interpretive summary.
suggestions: Retain the concrete ultrasound findings and close filling-versus-ejection-fraction alternative. Clinical sign-off should confirm the exact protocol ranking.

review.title: Classify nipple discharge patterns
fairness: The competing medication-associated bilateral expressed discharge and spontaneous unilateral component require separate interpretation; an elevated prolactin does not resolve both.

The four options cross the same two decisions symmetrically, so repeated phrases do not uniquely converge on the key. Medication review before pituitary imaging is plausible in this described exposure; the actual prolactin value and neurologic context would matter if the task demanded definitive endocrine disposition.
The key orders continued evaluation rather than claiming a cancer diagnosis. Exactly one offered combined plan is best on the stated information.
suggestions: Keep the mixed pattern and balanced option construction. Do not turn the red-brown drop into an explicit diagnosis or state that metoclopramide explains all discharge.

review.title: Select diagnostic imaging for pathologic discharge
fairness: Requires distinguishing an implant-integrity MRI protocol from evaluation of spontaneous focal discharge, then selecting the age-appropriate initial diagnostic pathway.

Silicone-sensitive sequences, absent contrast and intact shells are necessary protocol observations rather than a supplied 'inadequate study' conclusion. All options include ultrasound and differ in the complementary study.
The key is defensible if the outside implant MRI is the only prior imaging for this complaint. The current fields do not explicitly establish whether diagnostic mammography was also done.
suggestions: Add a neutral record of prior mammography/targeted ultrasound if the encounter can include earlier outside studies; do not call the implant MRI inconclusive. Preserve this as a protocol-application item.

review.title: Perioperative ART continuity
fairness: Recognizing the boosted regimen and distinguishing oral from monitored titrated intravenous midazolam requires pharmacology beyond wording recognition. The proposed oral route tempts a real error rather than repeating the key.
The four labels have parallel structure and balanced components. The key is a plan for titrated monitored administration, not a fixed dose or an assertion that interaction disappears intravenously.
The exact route-specific prescribing restrictions need clinician/source confirmation outside this no-network review; no confident inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain named drugs and route-specific alternatives; ensure clinical approval covers the precise intravenous-monitoring wording.

review.title: Boosted ART and midazolam

cues.phrase: the capnography trace becomes infrequent and chest movements become shallower
cues.why: Overt respiratory deterioration makes repeating the sedative unattractive even through ordinary safety reasoning; half the options fall without identifying the booster interaction.

cues.phrase: Repeat midazolam; assess and support ventilation; continue ART
cues.why: This bundles further sedation with support of visibly worsening ventilation. It reads as a deliberately contradictory plan; the other repeat-midazolam option has the same weakness.

fairness: Pausing sedation and supporting ventilation is a defensible immediate response; unchanged saturation on supplemental oxygen is a valid observation and should remain.
The residual ART choice is a separate continuity rule. Two binary actions do not create a difficult linked inference, and the immediate response would be the same with many sedating regimens.
Too easy for routine PGY-2/3 assessment; it is not basic-labelled.
suggestions: Keep the safety signs but replace the two implausible repeat-dose plans with credible supportive-care plans differing in the interaction-related next action or monitoring strategy.

Alternatively assess preventive sedation planning from actual medication reconciliation before deterioration, with clinically verified route/agent alternatives. Do not create difficulty by withholding respiratory deterioration.

review.title: Manometric recognition of achalasia
fairness: The elevated junction relaxation pressure and absence of a propagated contraction support the keyed broad diagnosis. The distractors are neighboring motility diagnoses and similarly styled.
This is classic pattern recognition, not two-step application; too easy as routine resident assessment.

ACCEPT_BASIC: one introductory pressure-tracing recognition item can establish the vocabulary needed for the discordant-position, medication and secondary-cause applications in this packet. That is a concrete scaffold, not a blanket exception for every achalasia sibling.
suggestions: Restrict this version to the introductory manometry lesson; do not count it toward resident difficulty or duplicate it as repeated advanced practice.

fairness: High-resolution manometry is the conventional next classification investigation after the supplied structural assessment; functional lumen imaging is a credible complementary test. No clear key reversal identified.

review.title: Dynamic ultrasound after an equivocal inguinal-hernia examination

cues.phrase: a separate surface swelling that is absent on waking
cues.why: The time/posture pattern favors the uniquely 'Standing' label. This is a weak positional hint, not a complete nonmedical distinction from dynamic MRI.

fairness: Dynamic ultrasound is a defensible initial study for the intermittent groin contour change despite musculoskeletal findings. Dynamic MRI is a plausible alternative, particularly at a different workup stage; no unequivocal clinical error identified.
The stem explicitly establishes no prior imaging. This asks familiar initial-test selection, not two-step reasoning, and is too easy for typical PGY-2/3 residents.
REJECT_BASIC: preserving the initial-test objective does not supply an onboarding purpose. Four nearly identical first-test items should not consume the difficulty exception.
suggestions: Use a technically specified prior examination, such as a negative supine scan performed without provocation, and require choosing an adequate repeat dynamic study versus MRI after an adequate negative study. Supply actual protocol and symptom observations, not the word 'inconclusive'.
Make siblings differ in imaging adequacy or symptom/imaging concordance rather than occupation, age or exertion trigger; re-version the objective if needed.

review.title: Elective planning for symptomatic inguinal hernia

cues.phrase: Pain at this site repeatedly interrupts the patient's usual activity.
cues.why: This states the standard symptom-burden rationale for elective consultation immediately before the choice. It largely resolves the competing watchful-waiting option; it is necessary decision information, so the repair is a harder decision, not deletion of the symptom burden.

fairness: The ultrasound supports a reducible inguinal hernia, and consultation is reasonable when symptoms limit activity. Coexisting musculoskeletal pain is not thereby disproved; consultation should not promise all pain will resolve after repair.
The already established diagnosis plus a classic symptom threshold yields one familiar management rule, not a demanding two-step task.
REJECT_BASIC: the justification identifies a narrow objective but no actual tutorial function; all four companions repeat the same update and answer.
suggestions: Create a symptom-attribution application: give precise locations and triggers for the patient's limiting pain and observed bulge, including concordant or discordant reproduction during ultrasound/examination. Ask for the next management discussion among repair assessment, targeted musculoskeletal evaluation and observation.
Supply patient goals and operative-risk facts only if they change the decision; use them to support competing plans rather than simply announce a desire for repair.

review.title: Map DTC with preoperative neck ultrasound
fairness: Papillary-type cytology and a lateral node make preoperative compartment mapping a defensible next step. Close nodule-only aspiration images do not establish that mapping was performed.
Recognizing the cytology and reciting the routine initial mapping test is highly familiar to residents. The apparent two steps do not create a real competing interpretation or management error.
REJECT_BASIC: 'basic preoperative workup rule' names the easy content, not a rare onboarding purpose. No specific tutorial role is shown.
suggestions: Give an actual prior neck ultrasound with documented compartments, node observations and an incomplete sampled target; ask which additional mapping or tissue-confirmation step changes the operative plan.
Use supported node features and explicit prior coverage rather than inventing a size cutoff or substituting another age.

review.title: Escalate complicated stoma prolapse

cues.phrase: cannot be gently returned
cues.why: Directly weakens another manual-reduction attempt.

cues.phrase: cramping, vomiting and much less stoma output
cues.why: Even a nonexpert can favor hospital care over two outpatient-disposition options from this severity pattern. These are necessary warning signs, not gratuitous cues to delete.

fairness: Urgent surgical assessment and fluids are defensible for the described irreducible prolapse with obstructive symptoms. Red color alone should not be presented as proof of ischemia, and the key does not do so.
ACCEPT_BASIC: appropriate as a rare introductory escalation/safety lesson teaching when clinic management must stop. Explicitly easy; it should not count toward the resident difficulty target.
Do not disguise the obstruction or failed reduction to make this item harder.
suggestions: Place once in early clinic-escalation onboarding and preserve the red flags. A subsequent advanced case can test management after initial stabilization, with verified findings and genuinely competing actions.

review.title: Sentinel-node staging discussion for melanoma
fairness: The resident must reject false reassurance from benign-appearing nodes and then coordinate sentinel staging with primary-site surgery before reconstruction. The normal basin ultrasound is needed to test this misconception.
The timing alternatives are coherent and similar in length. No direct lexical route identifies the key; knowing that reconstruction can complicate later mapping is doing meaningful work.

The keyed sequence is defensible; the delayed option should be treated as less appropriate, not as a claim that later mapping is invariably impossible. The narrow diagnostic-closure observation does not preclude a larger definitive defect.
suggestions: Retain the node observations and planned reconstruction. Remove the earlier lax-skin sentence from this management task if it has no continuing display purpose.

review.title: Complete diagnostic biopsy of a suspicious pigmented lesion

cues.phrase: the surrounding lax skin can be brought together around the entire lesion without tension
cues.why: This is effectively permission for the key's 'Entire-lesion excision', and repeats 'entire lesion'. A nonmedical reader can match whole-lesion closure feasibility to the one whole-lesion option.

cues.phrase: Entire-lesion excision with narrow margin into subcutaneous fat
cues.why: The key uniquely specifies a margin and changes sampling category; the other two are near-duplicate punch plans differing only in focus. This isolates the comprehensive option.

fairness: Complete appropriately deep diagnostic sampling is defensible when the whole lesion can be removed safely; the feasibility information is clinically relevant and cannot simply be deleted while retaining competing techniques.
The two punch options are weakly separated; selecting a complete specimen is familiar recognition, too easy for routine resident assessment.
REJECT_BASIC: four copies of the same complete-biopsy rule do not have four distinct introductory roles. The justification does not establish why this is needed in onboarding.
suggestions: Use an actual incomplete specimen whose deep edge, residual raised component and pathology prevent reliable microstaging; ask which targeted completion strategy resolves the uncertainty before definitive staging.

Alternatively use a genuinely constrained site with explicit lesion dimensions and closure limits, then offer clinically defensible sampling approaches. Obtain clinician-supported technique criteria; do not make a correct complete excision wrong by hidden constraints.

review.title: Sentinel-node staging discussion for melanoma

cues.phrase: no palpable node; ultrasound of the basin shows oval nodes with preserved central hilar echoes
cues.why: This strongly reduces the appeal of biopsying an imaged node. It is appropriate staging information, but with only ultrasound surveillance as the other competitor the item becomes a basic sentinel-node rule.

fairness: Sentinel-node staging discussion is defensible for the stated thickness and clinically negative basin. Normal ultrasound does not establish absence of microscopic disease.
Histologic wording for melanoma followed by an uncomplicated above-threshold thickness is recognition plus recall, not genuinely difficult two-step application.
REJECT_BASIC: the two above-threshold variants repeat a rule already exercised in the applied timing siblings; the justification explicitly describes simplicity without a tutorial purpose.
suggestions: Introduce an actual discrepancy between primary-specimen completeness and measured thickness, or a suspicious regional node with a documented sampling result, and ask how it changes the next staging action.
Specify the decisive histologic or nodal observations and have Melissa verify the relevant criteria. Do not invent a borderline numeric threshold.

fairness: Complete appropriately deep diagnostic sampling is defensible when the whole lesion can be removed safely; the feasibility information is clinically relevant and cannot simply be deleted while retaining competing techniques.
The two punch options are weakly separated; selecting a complete specimen is familiar recognition, too easy for routine resident assessment.
REJECT_BASIC: four copies of the same complete-biopsy rule do not have four distinct introductory roles. The justification does not establish why this is needed in onboarding.
suggestions: Use an actual incomplete specimen whose deep edge, residual raised component and pathology prevent reliable microstaging; ask which targeted completion strategy resolves the uncertainty before definitive staging.

Alternatively use a genuinely constrained site with explicit lesion dimensions and closure limits, then offer clinically defensible sampling approaches. Obtain clinician-supported technique criteria; do not make a correct complete excision wrong by hidden constraints.

review.title: Sentinel-node staging discussion for melanoma

cues.phrase: no palpable node; ultrasound of the basin shows oval nodes with preserved central hilar echoes
cues.why: This strongly reduces the appeal of biopsying an imaged node. It is appropriate staging information, but with only ultrasound surveillance as the other competitor the item becomes a basic sentinel-node rule.

fairness: Sentinel-node staging discussion is defensible for the stated thickness and clinically negative basin. Normal ultrasound does not establish absence of microscopic disease.
Histologic wording for melanoma followed by an uncomplicated above-threshold thickness is recognition plus recall, not genuinely difficult two-step application.
REJECT_BASIC: the two above-threshold variants repeat a rule already exercised in the applied timing siblings; the justification explicitly describes simplicity without a tutorial purpose.
suggestions: Introduce an actual discrepancy between primary-specimen completeness and measured thickness, or a suspicious regional node with a documented sampling result, and ask how it changes the next staging action.
Specify the decisive histologic or nodal observations and have Melissa verify the relevant criteria. Do not invent a borderline numeric threshold.

review.title: Management of a clearly characterized asymptomatic colonic lipoma
fairness: The resident must integrate endoscopic texture, submucosal-layer origin and echogenicity into a confident benign diagnosis, then distinguish no lesion-directed care from reflex sampling, resection or surveillance.

review.title: Endoscopic recognition of colonic lipoma

cues.phrase: without internal fluid spaces
cues.why: Selectively weakens the lymphangioma distractor on top of several already classic lipoma findings. This needs medical knowledge, but overdetermines this simple classification rather than creating a second inference.

fairness: The integrated soft yellow lesion and third-layer uniformly bright appearance support lipoma. No clear key reversal identified.
Classical single-diagnosis recognition is easy for the target audience, and the two context versions are substantively identical.

suggestions: Test interpretation of a discordant wall-layer or internal-echo observation before accepting the apparent cushion sign; ask what further characterization or sampling would resolve that discrepancy.

review.title: Avoid routine prophylactic splenectomy in proximal gastric cancer
fairness: Requires interpreting depth and location to choose nodal dissection extent, then distinguishing oncologic lymphadenectomy from routine removal of an uninvolved spleen.
The preserved fat plane and lesser-curvature location are decision-critical anatomy; neither gives a lay reader the D1-versus-D2 answer. The four options symmetrically cross both operative choices.

The key is defensible as an operative component for appropriately staged resectable disease. The vignette does not establish the entire multimodal treatment sequence, fitness or absence of distant disease; do not interpret it as authorizing immediate surgery.

review.title: Pathologic recognition of gastric MALT lymphoma

cues.phrase: glands pass through the infiltrate with their epithelium preserved
cues.why: This emphasizes the absent classic destructive feature and points toward a specimen/architecture problem, but does not establish why a new endoscopy is superior to testing the tissue already available.

fairness: Hardness here partly reflects an unresolved diagnostic-workup ranking, not a well-specified two-step decision. A clonal B-cell population is not by itself a definitive morphologic diagnosis.

No sample adequacy, mapping distribution, expert pathology conclusion or remaining material is given. BIRC3-MALT1 testing on existing material is an arguably defensible clarifying investigation; the stem does not show why it should be displaced by repeat endoscopy.

I am not asserting that fusion testing is necessarily preferred, or that repeat endoscopy is wrong. Without source checking, I cannot establish one best answer between these plausible pathways. The exact key must be adjudicated by Melissa/pathology before passing.
suggestions: State the actual biopsy adequacy and distribution, remaining tissue availability and the unresolved pathology question. If the intended problem is nonrepresentative mucosal sampling, provide raw evidence of that limitation.
Choose distractors that are verifiably inferior at that stage, or reframe the decision around what the existing findings do and do not establish. Do not claim preserved glands exclude MALT lymphoma.

review.title: H. pylori eradication as initial treatment for localized gastric MALT lymphoma

cues.phrase: H. pylori eradication with planned histologic response assessment
cues.why: The key combines the eradication component shared with one distractor and the planned-assessment structure shared with the other. This partial convergence can reward choosing the apparent combination of the two 'good' halves.

fairness: The explicitly diagnosed localized H. pylori-positive disease supports eradication with planned histologic assessment. The symptom-only follow-up alternative is a meaningful error but a familiar one.
The diagnosis, infection and extent are already supplied; selecting the first-line therapy and its standard follow-up is routine recall rather than a challenging causal sequence.
Too easy for routine residents and not basic-labelled. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the key.
suggestions: Move to a documented post-eradication assessment: give infection-test conditions, histologic trajectory, symptoms and staging observations, then ask whether to reassess, observe or escalate. Have the clinician establish the evidence-supported time/response boundary.
Make options complete, parallel treatment-and-assessment plans without a key that simply combines repeated components; do not invent an exact response deadline.

review.title: Pathologic recognition of gastric MALT lymphoma

cues.phrase: CD5, CD10 and cyclin D1 do not
cues.why: The negative marker list is tailored to exclude the two named lymphoma competitors. These are valid diagnostic observations, but with the gland-infiltration pattern they turn the item into a heavily cued marker-recognition table rather than an application.

fairness: The supplied integrated B-cell and gland-infiltration pattern supports the keyed lymphoma among the three choices. Marker negativity alone should not be taught as sufficient for classification.
The full marginal-zone label is naturally longer, not a reliable grammar/length trick by itself. No clinical inaccuracy confidently identified.
REJECT_BASIC: maintaining a narrow pathology objective and pointing to a management companion do not justify repeated introductory recognition. This is easy for the intended resident use.
suggestions: Test what can be concluded from a genuinely limited or discordant specimen and what additional comparison is needed, rather than simply listing the signature positive and negative markers.

Alternatively integrate an original pathology interpretation with a documented clinical staging or response decision. Give the decisive morphology and verified criteria, and version changed clinical meaning explicitly.

review.title: Interpret a p-value

cues.phrase: It confirms a benefit of at least 4 percentage points only if the entire reported 95% interval reaches at least that reduction
cues.why: The stem supplies the exact target-benefit comparison rule before an interval crossing zero. Together with the explicit alpha this permits two straightforward numerical comparisons rather than a difficult interpretation.

fairness: The key is statistically defensible: p=0.4 does not reject the stated null, and the interval does not establish the target benefit. It also does not exclude that benefit; 'unconfirmed' must not be taught as 'absent'.
The fictional threshold and protocol must be supplied for fairness. The problem is that this wide interval offers no meaningful tension between the two decisions, not that the protocol is visible.
Two separately cued threshold checks are not genuine two-step resident reasoning. Too easy and not basic-labelled.
suggestions: Preserve the protocol but present a real interpretive conflict, such as a point estimate meeting the benefit target with a compatible interval also admitting harm, and ask which claim or next study-planning decision is justified.
Use options that distinguish benefit unconfirmed from benefit excluded; do not make failure to reject the null synonymous with equivalence.

review.title: Interpret a p-value
fairness: The effect estimate exceeds the target and the null is rejected, yet the interval also permits benefits smaller than the target. Separating statistical evidence from support for the prespecified magnitude is a credible resident error.
The constructed criteria must remain explicit; their presence is not an unfair teaching cue when the question tests applying a declared protocol to discordant conclusions.
The keyed paired conclusion is defensible. Symmetric four-option construction does not favor a unique phrase.
suggestions: Keep the mismatch between point estimate, null testing and magnitude support. Avoid feedback that interprets 'unconfirmed' as 'ruled out'.

review.title: Distinguish risk ratio and odds ratio
fairness: The learner must translate baseline risk to odds, apply the conditional odds ratio, then translate back; directly multiplying 40% by 0.60 produces the credible 24% distractor.
With the fixed same-profile reference risk the calculation is well specified: (0.60*0.40)/(0.60+0.60*0.40)=0.285714..., approximately 29%.
The three numerical labels are parallel. No wording-only key, clinical threshold or marginal-versus-conditional ambiguity is apparent.
suggestions: Retain the fixed same-covariate-profile wording; it prevents an otherwise important adjusted-versus-marginal interpretation problem.

review.title: Arrange adult support after endoscopic sedation

cues.phrase: A driver who only drives does not fulfil that care role.
cues.why: Explicitly eliminates both driver-only options, so half the answer is supplied verbatim by the protocol.

cues.phrase: A suitable adult accepts clinical handover, accompanies the patient home and can provide early recovery support.
cues.why: Restates the escort-and-handover component of the key. Appropriate for orientation, but not evidence of resident-level reasoning.

fairness: The escort requirement is unambiguous under this constructed protocol. It is a unit-specific rule, not a universal transport-policy claim.

The recovery half is underdetermined: the patient is now oriented and walking, but there is no observation interval, serial assessment or statement that the required post-reversal assessment is incomplete. Both continuing and ending recovery can be defensible depending on those missing facts.
ACCEPT_BASIC: applying a plainly displayed discharge/escort workflow is a valid early safety/onboarding purpose. This accepts the educational role, not the current recovery key or clinical approval.
suggestions: State that the unit-required post-reversal assessment has not yet been completed, or give the actual protocol criterion and observed recovery course. Do not invent a universal observation duration.
Alternatively remove the end-versus-continue recovery axis and test only transport/handover after documented satisfactory recovery. Keep this as a rare onboarding item.

review.title: Interpret a p-value
fairness: The superiority p-value does not reject the null, and the supplied 90% interval does not lie within the declared equivalence margins. Failure to show superiority cannot substitute for demonstrating equivalence.
Distinguishing the two-sided superiority assessment from the two one-sided equivalence framework is a meaningful second inference. Symmetric choices avoid a wording shortcut.

'Uncertain' is less precise than 'not demonstrated' but does not make another option correct. The lower side of the interval extending beyond the negative equivalence margin is enough to prevent equivalence support.
suggestions: Prefer 'superiority not demonstrated; equivalence not demonstrated' consistently across choices to align the claim with the protocol. Preserve both confidence levels and explicit margins.

review.title: Endoscopic drainage referral for a symptomatic pseudocyst
fairness: Two clinical inferences are available: recognize a mature fluid-only post-pancreatitis collection, then connect gastric apposition and symptoms to a drainage route. Both are classic and largely unopposed here; this is too easy for the routine resident difficulty target.

The degree, trajectory and nutritional consequence of early fullness/reduced intake are insufficiently described to decisively rank referral for drainage against observation with nutritional support. Referral for assessment is reasonable, but the item should not imply any persistent fullness mandates drainage.

The key is referral for assessment, not immediate puncture; vascular and ductal evaluation can occur during that assessment. Do not automatically fail the referral solely because a complete preprocedure safety workup is absent.
All four sibling cases use essentially the same anatomy and options. No reliable nonmedical wording/length shortcut identified; the failure is insufficient challenge plus unresolved symptom severity.
suggestions: Give observed intake/weight or vomiting trajectory and any prior supportive-management response so the need for intervention can be judged rather than assumed.

To create a harder application, supply actual imaging observations that alter the otherwise reasonable drainage plan, such as a vascular finding along the proposed tract or uncertain fluid-versus-solid contents. Ask for the next assessment or sequence among genuinely plausible options.
Use clinician-verified findings and criteria; do not add arbitrary size, maturation or drainage thresholds. Vary the decision across siblings rather than just symptoms and age.

review.title: Contrast CT characterization of a pancreatic fluid collection

cues.phrase: Abdominal CT: intravenous contrast given; oral contrast omitted
cues.why: Only one option offers intravenous enhancement; the other two differ solely in oral contrast. The three-label format therefore collapses to a basic IV-contrast yes/no rule, with the key a component outlier rather than a complex protocol choice.

fairness: An IV-enhanced abdominal CT is a defensible characterization study if contrast is appropriate. The exact oral-contrast omission is not justified by the visible findings; its inclusion should not teach that oral contrast is universally inappropriate.
The task supplies the modality and asks a single contrast-route distinction, too easy for routine PGY-2/3 assessment.
REJECT_BASIC: four copies of a basic contrast rule are not supported by an introductory/interface function. Keeping a companion unchanged is not a difficulty justification.
suggestions: Give a concrete prior acquisition and an unresolved vascular, ductal or debris question, then ask which targeted imaging protocol resolves it before intervention.
Use comparably credible protocols and state eligibility when it matters; obtain source/clinician support for the requested phase or modality. Do not add unsupported scan phases or fixed timing.

review.title: Act and iterate after a PDSA test

cues.phrase: Medication-list entry: total minutes
cues.why: The sole workload increase is in this row (10 to 50), and only the key changes medication-field entry. Simple table matching identifies the answer without clinical or QI knowledge.

cues.phrase: Prefill medication fields; retain escalation prompts
cues.why: Only the key acts on the conspicuous outlier; both alternatives change escalation despite unchanged escalation time and perfect recorded agreement.

cues.phrase: they do not establish a causal treatment effect
cues.why: This pre-answer methods teaching is unnecessary to choose among the three process modifications. It should be in feedback unless causal interpretation is actually tested.

fairness: Testing prefill is a reasonable hypothesis for the observed workload issue; accuracy of manually entered data does not establish accuracy of a proposed prefill source.
The key proposes another small test, so the absence of demonstrated prefill benefit is not itself a fatal fairness flaw. However, availability and provenance of a prefill source are not given.
Too easy for residents: spotting one increased table cell and matching a label is not a meaningful two-step QI decision.
suggestions: Give a plausible benefit/burden tradeoff or stratified process data that distinguish two potential causes of the extra time; require choosing a small test that would discriminate them.
If prefill remains an option, specify the available source and known reconciliation limitations. Offer other changes addressing the same bottleneck, with observations that select one fairly.
Move the causal-effect teaching sentence to feedback unless it is the object of the question.

review.title: Tissue confirmation of inflammatory breast cancer

cues.phrase: no tissue block is available
cues.why: Announces the need for tissue architecture after an atypical aspirate, making a core-type approach an obvious upgrade. This is legitimate specimen information, but the standard sampling rule remains simple.

cues.phrase: External systemic staging is planned if invasive carcinoma is confirmed.
cues.why: Previews the purpose of the next tissue step without changing the choice among the three sampling techniques; it is an unnecessary sequencing hint.

fairness: Core sampling of the parenchymal target is a defensible next step for establishing invasive carcinoma and obtaining tissue for characterization. Skin sampling can be complementary but should not be taught as an interchangeable substitute or as never indicated.
The stem supplies a target accessible to ultrasound, an inadequate aspirate and classic inflammatory features. The open-incision competitor is weak for routine initial sampling.

REJECT_BASIC: preserving a harder management companion does not establish a need for this easy introductory rule. The narrow tissue-confirmation objective should not excuse the resident difficulty gap.
suggestions: Develop a documented imaging-pathology discordance after a specific biopsy, then require selecting the next specimen/site or review step. Supply targeting, adequacy and morphology rather than an 'inconclusive' summary.
Keep any essential raw evidence of specimen limitation, but remove the future staging sentence if it has no independent task function.

review.title: Neoadjuvant sequence for stage III inflammatory breast cancer
fairness: The resident must recognize the initial inflammatory presentation, then resist de-escalating local treatment solely because systemic therapy removes visible and palpable abnormalities.
The response is explicitly conditional, preserving chronology. The key and breast-conserving alternative are comparable complete local-treatment plans and require clinical knowledge to distinguish.

The key is defensible for the stated nonmetastatic inflammatory phenotype. Exact sequencing and patient eligibility require clinician approval; the item does not specify a drug regimen or imply every skin-redness presentation is inflammatory cancer.

review.title: Interpret a confidence interval
fairness: The learner must translate the whole relative-risk interval using the fixed control risk, then compare its upper absolute-risk difference with the hypothetical harm margin.

The transformed interval is (0.40-1)*20=-12 to (1.20-1)*20=+4 percentage points; +5 lies outside. The first distractor retains the same conclusion with a wrong interval, so shortcutting directly to the conclusion does not identify the key.
Fixed reference-risk wording avoids an unaddressed second estimated quantity. The conclusion is about this reported interval, not certainty that the true risk cannot exceed the margin.
suggestions: Retain the fixed-risk caveat and parallel numerical alternatives. Feedback should distinguish an interval-model conclusion from proof of no harm.

review.title: Interpret a p-value
fairness: The resident must separate strong evidence against zero effect from an interval whose entire magnitude falls short of the protocol's target. This tests the common significance-equals-importance error.

The key is correct under the explicit constructed criteria: the null is rejected, and a one-percentage-point reduction is outside the reported interval. It does not establish a clinical threshold for real thyroid surgery.

The criteria are necessary context for a hypothetical protocol, not an automatic cue violation. All four options are balanced; this is moderate at most and less demanding after the parallel statistics siblings.
suggestions: Keep the effect-size conflict and explicit fictional-protocol status. Avoid near-consecutive repeated exposure to B27/B39 as though it measures independent hard reasoning.

review.title: High-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata requiring endoscopic hemostasis
fairness: The nonbleeding visible vessel warrants a treatment decision despite the dry field. The clip-plus-acid-suppression key is defensible among the offered modalities; the item does not provide a reason to rank it above every other accepted definitive modality.

The task tests a familiar visible-vessel/definitive-modality rule. No major nonmedical option-style cue is apparent, but the injection and powder competitors are easy for residents familiar with this rule.

REJECT_BASIC: explaining why several definitive therapies should not be placed in one ambiguous option set does not establish an onboarding purpose. A rare safety exception is already served more directly by the stoma-escalation case.
suggestions: Build an application around recurrent bleeding after a documented initial endoscopic course, with hemodynamics, actual target access and prior modalities sufficient to distinguish repeat endoscopy from interventional or operative referral.
Have Melissa verify the exact escalation boundary. Do not manufacture lesion-specific contraindications or choose between equally accepted modalities without deciding information.

review.title: Endoscopic hemostasis modality selection for peptic-ulcer bleeding

cues.phrase: Epinephrine injection stops the oozing

cues.phrase: The endoscopist maintains a stable front-on view of the exposed vessel.
cues.why: Supplies favorable access for the only offered contact treatment. This is useful eligibility information, but combined with the failed clip and stopped oozing it largely walks the learner to the intended modality.

fairness: The same duodenal lesion is maintained, and procedural oozing can occur after an initially dry field; no necessary continuity contradiction.

Contact bipolar treatment is defensible after the failed clip and injection-controlled bleeding if technically suitable. The decision mainly recalls injection-plus-another-modality, rather than resolving a difficult rescue question. REJECT_BASIC: the justification acknowledges simplicity but establishes no introductory role.
suggestions: Move to a verified rebleeding or technical-access problem in which at least two escalation routes are initially credible, and give the decisive procedural findings.

question.stem: Which measure is calculated by the expression in this ulcer-recurrence report?

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes the ratio of two odds, rather than a direct comparison of probabilities.

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio
answerChoices.rationale: Treats division of odds as though it were division of the probabilities themselves.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Treats division of odds as though it were division of the probabilities themselves.

answerChoices.label: Risk difference
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses a relative comparison with subtraction of the two probabilities.

question.explanation: Each p/(1-p) term is an odds. Dividing the two terms produces an odds ratio. A risk ratio divides the probabilities themselves, and a risk difference subtracts them. Similarity in selected settings does not make these measures interchangeable.
question.teachingPoint: Each p/(1-p) term is an odds. Dividing the two terms produces an odds ratio. A risk ratio divides the probabilities themselves, and a risk difference subtracts them. Similarity in selected settings does not make these measures interchangeable.

question.stem: Which diagnostic sampling plan should be used for {patientName}'s skin lesion?

answerChoices.label: Entire-lesion excision with narrow margin into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.rationale: Provides whole-lesion architecture and adequate depth when the stated site/closure findings permit diagnostic excision.

answerChoices.label: Punch biopsy of the darkest pigmented focus into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Provides depth at one focus but can miss relevant architecture or a different invasive focus elsewhere.

answerChoices.label: Punch biopsy of the most elevated focus into subcutaneous fat

question.explanation: A narrow diagnostic excision of the entire small lesion into subcutaneous fat provides architecture and depth for assessment. question.stem: Which treatment plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s resection site?

answerChoices.label: Segmental colectomy with removal of the draining mesentery
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the adverse invasive-polyp feature and recognizes a regional-node risk that a clear-looking scar or negative CT cannot remove.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness excision centered on the resection scar
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Addresses potential local residual disease but does not provide regional nodal treatment/staging for this adverse histology.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic scar surveillance with repeat targeted tissue sampling
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Overweights endoscopic/CT reassurance and does not address the adverse histologic feature that changes the adequacy of polypectomy.

question.explanation: An endoscopically removed malignant polyp is not automatically cured by a clear-looking scar. The supplied adverse invasive feature supports discussion of oncologic resection with the regional mesentery. CT-negative nodes do not exclude microscopic disease. Exact bowel extent, especially for a transverse lesion, remains an anatomic operative decision.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnosis fits {patientName}'s endoscopic and wall-layer observations?

answerChoices.label: Colonic lipoma
answerChoices.rationale: Combines compressibility/yellow surface with a uniform hyperechoic submucosal lesion.

answerChoices.label: Colonic lymphangioma
answerChoices.rationale: Can be deformable and submucosal, but ordinarily has fluid-containing/cystic internal spaces rather than the supplied uniform bright solid pattern.

answerChoices.label: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
answerChoices.rationale: Is a plausible solid subepithelial alternative, but the usual muscularis-propria hypoechoic pattern differs from these observations.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next investigation should clarify {patientName}'s gastric infiltrate?

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopy with documented-site biopsies for histologic comparison
answerChoices.rationale: Resolves integrated diagnostic uncertainty instead of treating a clone plus lineage as established MALT lymphoma.

answerChoices.label: BIRC3-MALT1 fusion testing on the recorded gastric biopsy material
answerChoices.rationale: Is useful in established gastric MALT evaluation but does not alone resolve the current morphologic classification.

answerChoices.label: Repeat immunoglobulin gene-rearrangement analysis on a second DNA extraction
answerChoices.rationale: Can corroborate a clone but does not convert clonality without characteristic morphology into a lymphoma diagnosis.

decisionNodes.explanation: B-cell lineage and a clonal rearrangement need morphologic/clinical correlation: chronic inflammation can contain clonal B-cell expansions. The preserved gland epithelium in this sampled infiltrate does not supply the characteristic destructive gland interaction. Repeat documented biopsies and comparative expert review are appropriate for diagnostic uncertainty. Fusion testing and repeat clonality can contribute, but do not replace that assessment.

cases.learningSummary:
Active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel are high-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata that warrant endoscopic hemostasis. A clean base or flat pigmented spot does not require endoscopic treatment solely for that finding.

For a nonbleeding visible vessel, accepted thermal or mechanical therapy may be used alone or with epinephrine. Epinephrine alone is not definitive hemostasis, while two definitive modalities are not automatically required.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial imaging study should be arranged for {patientName}'s groin symptoms?

answerChoices.label: Standing groin ultrasound during straining
answerChoices.rationale: Targets the intermittent protrusion at the initial imaging stage.

answerChoices.label: Dynamic groin MRI during straining
answerChoices.rationale: Is a credible problem-solving option, rather than a hip-only protocol deliberately prevented from assessing the reported protrusion.

answerChoices.label: Pelvic CT with multiplanar groin assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Is an anatomic alternative, but not the preferred initial dynamic study in the represented stable setting.

decisionNodes.explanation: The pain findings and intermittent swelling need not have the same explanation. Initial dynamic groin ultrasound can evaluate a lump that disappears at rest. Persistent uncertainty after an adequate assessment can require further investigation; MRI is not dismissed as an invalid alternative in every occult-hernia pathway.

answerChoices.label: Elective hernia repair consultation
answerChoices.rationale: Discusses repair without assuming all coexisting hip pain will disappear.

answerChoices.label: Watchful waiting with symptom-triggered review
answerChoices.rationale: Treats activity-limiting symptoms as though the patient were minimally symptomatic.

answerChoices.rationale: Overattributes the separate surface-swelling pain to a coexisting musculoskeletal finding.

The stable presentation does not require emergency treatment or a specific technique selection.

decisionNodes.stem: Which motility diagnosis fits {patientName}'s pressure tracing?

answerChoices.label: Achalasia
answerChoices.rationale: Integrates the body-pressure/contraction distinction with the appropriate junction-relaxation criterion; an apparent pressure event is not automatically normal peristalsis.

answerChoices.label: Esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction
answerChoices.rationale: Represents a competing motility classification; check whether its relaxation and true-peristalsis requirements fit all of the reported observations.

answerChoices.label: Distal esophageal spasm
answerChoices.rationale: Represents a competing motility classification; check whether its relaxation and true-peristalsis requirements fit all of the reported observations.

decisionNodes.explanation: Simultaneous pressurization does not establish a propagated contraction. Integrating absent true peristalsis with impaired junction relaxation supports achalasia rather than preserved-peristalsis outflow obstruction or spasm.

decisionNodes.stem: Which interpretation and planning decision should follow {patientName}'s study?

answerChoices.label: Conclusive achalasia pattern; arrange junction-directed treatment assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Complete failed peristalsis with abnormal primary-position relaxation pressure meets the classification despite a normal secondary-position pressure.

answerChoices.label: Inconclusive outflow-obstruction pattern; obtain corroboration before treatment assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Overapplies the both-position EGJOO requirement to a patient with no preserved peristalsis.

answerChoices.label: Absent-contractility pattern; arrange reflux-directed management assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Treats the normal upright measurement as overriding the abnormal adequate primary-position study.

decisionNodes.explanation: All primary-position swallows fail and junction relaxation pressure is abnormal in that adequate series. A normal upright pressure does not impose the both-position EGJOO rule on this achalasia pattern. Arrange specialist treatment assessment rather than classifying the study as absent contractility or automatically inconclusive EGJOO.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: All primary-position swallows fail and junction relaxation pressure is abnormal in that adequate series. answerChoices.label: Achalasia-like spastic pattern; reassess after coordinated opioid withdrawal
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes the pattern and the potentially reversible medication-associated contribution before committing to irreversible therapy.

answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes the tracing but treats it as sufficient proof of a primary irreversible disorder despite a relevant drug exposure.

answerChoices.label: Distal-spasm pattern; coordinate opioid withdrawal and reassessment before myotomy planning
answerChoices.rationale: Notices the medication issue but ignores the abnormal junction relaxation when classifying the tracing.

answerChoices.rationale: Combines an incorrect relaxation-pattern classification with premature invasive treatment planning during the relevant exposure.

decisionNodes.explanation: The failed/premature body activity with impaired junction relaxation is an achalasia-like spastic pattern. Opioids can produce this phenotype; Chicago v4 advises studying off opioids when possible. Coordinate a clinically appropriate withdrawal/reassessment plan before treating this as established primary disease requiring myotomy. No abrupt cessation or fixed washout is prescribed.

answerChoices.label: Achalasia-pattern physiology; investigate a secondary junction lesion before treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes failed contractions and impaired relaxation while responding to the older patient's progressive weight loss and endoscopic resistance.

answerChoices.label: Achalasia-pattern physiology; proceed to treatment planning after the mucosal endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Correctly reads the pressure pattern but overstates what a mucosal examination without an intraluminal mass excludes.

answerChoices.rationale: Notices the alarm observations but counts subthreshold pressure deflections as retained effective contractions despite impaired relaxation.

answerChoices.rationale: Combines a mistaken interpretation of the contractile measurements with premature closure of the secondary-cause assessment.

decisionNodes.explanation: The very low contractile measurements represent failed contractions, not preserved effective peristalsis. Impaired junction relaxation yields an achalasia pattern, but substantial recent weight loss and marked scope resistance in this older patient warrant targeted secondary-cause assessment before treatment planning. A normal-looking mucosa does not exclude a mural or extrinsic lesion.

cases.learningSummary: After an adequate endoscopic structural assessment excludes obstruction and concerning pseudoachalasia, high-resolution manometry supplies the esophageal physiology needed to evaluate suspected achalasia. Absent peristalsis together with impaired EGJ relaxation supports achalasia. Basal sphincter pressure can vary, so recognition rests on the accepted physiologic pattern rather than a universally elevated basal pressure.

decisionNodes.stem: Which diagnostic sampling plan should be used for {patientName}'s skin lesion?

answerChoices.label: Entire-lesion excision with narrow margin into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.rationale: Provides whole-lesion architecture and adequate depth when the stated site/closure findings permit diagnostic excision.

answerChoices.label: Punch biopsy of the darkest pigmented focus into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.rationale: Provides depth at one focus but can miss relevant architecture or a different invasive focus elsewhere.

answerChoices.label: Punch biopsy of the most elevated focus into subcutaneous fat
answerChoices.rationale: Targets a plausible invasive focus but does not assess the whole small lesion when complete diagnostic excision is feasible.

decisionNodes.explanation: A narrow diagnostic excision of the entire small lesion into subcutaneous fat provides architecture and depth for assessment. Either full-depth focal punch can miss a different relevant component. This does not make focal sampling inappropriate for every large or anatomically constrained lesion; the supplied closure examination defines the represented feasible diagnostic excision.

decisionNodes.stem: Which combined primary-site and regional-node plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Sentinel-node biopsy with wide excision, before reconstructive closure
answerChoices.rationale: Maintains microscopic nodal staging and coordinates it with excision before the planned reconstruction can alter lymphatic mapping.

answerChoices.label: Sentinel-node biopsy after wide excision and reconstructive healing
answerChoices.rationale: Recognizes the staging indication but unnecessarily separates it until after a flap or graft can compromise mapping.

answerChoices.label: Nodal ultrasound surveillance after wide excision and reconstructive closure
answerChoices.rationale: Treats the reassuring sonographic basin as a substitute for indicated microscopic regional staging.

decisionNodes.explanation: Discuss sentinel-node staging for the represented clinically node-negative intermediate-thickness melanoma. Reassuring nodal ultrasound does not replace microscopic staging. Final surgical choices remain individualized.

decisionNodes.stem: Which regional-node assessment should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Sentinel lymph node mapping and biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: Interprets the primary depth and clinically uninvolved basin, rather than treating reassuring node imaging as exclusion of microscopic involvement.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided biopsy of an imaged regional node
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses size-selected sampling of a nonsuspicious visible node with mapping the sentinel drainage of the primary lesion.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound surveillance of the regional nodes
answerChoices.rationale: Overweights benign-appearing imaged nodes and omits the indicated pathologic sentinel staging discussion.

decisionNodes.explanation: The histology establishes an invasive melanoma with the supplied depth. In this clinically node-negative setting, sentinel-node staging should be discussed with definitive excision planning; sampling an arbitrary benign-appearing node or relying on surveillance does not supply equivalent sentinel staging.

decisionNodes.stem: Which imaging plan should complete {patientName}'s pretreatment assessment?

answerChoices.label: Thoracic CT to complete the existing cross-sectional staging
answerChoices.rationale: Completes the unassessed thorax rather than treating lung bases/chest radiography as full thoracic CT.

answerChoices.label: Hepatic MRI to complete the existing cross-sectional staging
answerChoices.rationale: Adds liver characterization despite no indeterminate lesion and leaves the thoracic staging gap.

answerChoices.label: Whole-body FDG PET-CT to replace the existing staging pathway
answerChoices.rationale: Escalates to routine metabolic staging rather than completing the standard anatomic assessment.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read both the coverage and acquisition of the prior study. Standard colon-cancer distant staging includes thoracic CT and adequate contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic assessment; a negative radiograph, organ ultrasound or PET uptake/localization report does not automatically supply that assessment. MRI is a legitimate abdominal alternative in appropriate pathways, not inherently a wrong test.

decisionNodes.stem: Which broad treatment plan should be discussed with {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Resection of the involved colon with its regional lymphatic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Addresses incompletely assessed invasive disease and regional risk after a malignant polyp with an involved deep margin, despite a clear scar and normal-size CT nodes.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic full-thickness removal of the colon scar and local wall
answerChoices.rationale: Could improve local wall assessment, but is not the preferred substitute for oncologic regional resection in this fit patient with involved/indeterminate invasive clearance.

answerChoices.label: Endoscopic colon scar surveillance with targeted mucosal tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: Mistakes a scar and reassuring CT for proof of local invasive clearance and microscopic node negativity.

decisionNodes.explanation: The deep invasive front is transected and local depth/clearance cannot be adequately assessed. In a surgically suitable patient, this is not the low-risk, completely excised malignant-polyp group. Discuss oncologic resection including regional lymphatic drainage; neither a clear scar nor normal-size CT nodes establishes clearance. This is a broad planning choice, not specification of the exact transverse-colon operation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which management plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s returned imaging findings and ongoing symptoms?

answerChoices.label: Referral for endoscopic transmural drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Retains the passed anatomy/symptom inference while requiring specialist assessment of vascular/access safety before any puncture.

answerChoices.label: Referral for percutaneous catheter drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Is a possible route in selected circumstances, but is not favored over endoscopic assessment for the supplied gastric apposition and burden.

answerChoices.label: Referral for operative internal drainage assessment
answerChoices.rationale: May be appropriate in selected anatomy or after other approaches fail; no such preference is established here.

answerChoices.label: Observation with nutritional support and repeat imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Is appropriate for some collections, but does not address the represented ongoing gastric compression/food-intake burden as well as specialist drainage planning.

decisionNodes.stem: Which tissue-sampling plan should be arranged next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the parenchymal target
answerChoices.rationale: Provides tissue from the imaged breast target for diagnosis and biomarkers, with skin punch as an adjunct rather than a substitute.

answerChoices.label: Open incisional sampling of the parenchymal abnormality
answerChoices.rationale: Can provide tissue but escalates to an open initial procedure when an imaged percutaneous target is supplied.

answerChoices.label: Multiple punch samples from the involved breast skin
answerChoices.rationale: Can give useful complementary evidence but is not an equivalent substitute for sampling the supplied parenchymal target.

decisionNodes.explanation: The rapidly evolving skin/breast findings warrant assessment of an invasive breast malignancy. The existing external pathway completes staging after confirmation, not because suspicion alone equals a cancer diagnosis.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial operation is most appropriate for {patientName}'s papillary thyroid carcinoma?

answerChoices.label: Lobectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Applies the 2025 ATA initial-surgery recommendation to the stated unilateral 2 cm, intrathyroidal, node-negative and nonmetastatic profile.

answerChoices.label: Total thyroidectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Extends treatment beyond the recommended initial extent for this stated profile without another supplied indication for contralateral surgery.

answerChoices.label: Subtotal thyroidectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Treats subtotal resection as an intermediate cancer operation; it is not the recommended initial operation for this profile.

decisionNodes.explanation: For the stated unilateral cancer measuring 2 cm without gross extension or nodal or distant metastases, the 2025 ATA recommendation supports lobectomy as the initial operation when surgery is chosen. Bilateral cancer or other indications can change the operation. This choice follows disease extent rather than an answer-directing tissue-preservation request.

decisionNodes.stem: Which examination protocol should be ordered next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assessing gallbladder filling
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent local inflammatory findings call for assessment of gallbladder filling/cystic-duct obstruction despite the ultrasound components.

answerChoices.rationale: Confuses evaluation of chronic gallbladder emptying with evaluation of the acute inflammatory presentation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which phosphate movement best accounts for the fall in serum phosphate during this nutrition restart?

answerChoices.label: From extracellular fluid into cells
answerChoices.rationale: Connects carbohydrate-driven insulin activity with cellular phosphate uptake.

answerChoices.label: From cells into extracellular fluid
answerChoices.rationale: Reverses the compartment shift and would tend to raise the measured extracellular concentration.

answerChoices.label: From circulating blood into urine
answerChoices.rationale: Mistakes an intracellular redistribution for renal loss after focusing on the falling serum result.

answerChoices.label: From intestinal lumen into blood
answerChoices.rationale: Confuses the source of newly absorbed nutrients with the redistribution explaining the serum fall.

decisionNodes.explanation: After prolonged undernutrition, carbohydrate-associated insulin activity can increase cellular phosphate uptake. The relevant movement is from extracellular fluid into cells; the serum result measures the extracellular compartment.

cases.learningSummary: The correct answer is “Continue ART with the perioperative team.” Routine surgery alone is not an indication to stop effective ART. Surgical recovery alone does not justify interrupting feasible ART. An uncoordinated single-drug substitute does not preserve the prescribed regimen. Uncoordinated removal of part of a regimen is not the continuity plan. The correct answer is “Revise sedation for the ART interaction.” Boosted therapy can increase midazolam exposure; this oral combination requires an alternative plan. The oral combination has a route-specific contraindication. Increased exposure from metabolic inhibition does not support a dose increase. A coordinated alternative sedation plan is preferable to sacrificing feasible effective ART.

decisionNodes.stem: Which next step is most appropriate for {patientName}'s recurrent peristomal skin injury?

answerChoices.label: Reassess pouch fit with the ostomy nurse
answerChoices.rationale: Uses the distribution and removed-appliance observations to prioritize assessment of the seal and fit before prescribing a particular product or opening dimension.

answerChoices.label: Switch to a different adhesive brand
answerChoices.rationale: Treats the complaint as an adhesive-product problem without first explaining the observed distribution and inner-edge moisture.

answerChoices.label: Start topical antifungal treatment
answerChoices.rationale: Treats a competing rash mechanism before assessing the appliance and the source of the recurrent contact injury.

answerChoices.label: Schedule more frequent routine pouch changes
answerChoices.rationale: May form part of an individualized plan, but selecting a new routine interval alone does not assess why this appliance repeatedly fails at the affected skin.
